entries.clue: Building unsecured if I certified locks (7)

indicatorNotes.locks: to lock something in is to hold it fast where it is, so the words in front of it keep the letters shut between them

blocks.note: the run begins two letters from the end of the first word, swallows both short ones whole and stops two letters into the last

annotation.surface: A building left insecure despite the locks somebody signed off as sound.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Unsecured' looks like an instruction to shake up the letters after it, and is really where the hidden run starts. Seven letters is long for a hidden word, so solvers give up scanning before they reach the end.
annotation.definitionFit: An edifice is a building, normally a large and imposing one, so the plain word covers it exactly.

entries.clue: Cavalryman with women's clothing on checks zip (7)

indicatorNotes.checks: to check a thing is to hold it back, and what is held back stays inside the letters doing the holding

blocks.note: drag is clothing of the opposite sex, in practice a man in women's clothes
the clue's own two letters, taken as they stand
zip is nothing at all, and nothing is written as O

annotation.surface: Women's clothing worn over checked fabric, with a zip.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word after the definition is doing a job the surface disguises as clothing: a fabric that checks, a fastener that is really nothing. Dragoons were mounted infantry, soldiers who rode to the battle and fought on foot.
annotation.definitionFit: A dragoon is a cavalryman, the soldier of a mounted regiment, and several British regiments still carry the name.

entries.clue: Halt progress following corrosion estimate (9)

blocks.note: f. is the reference abbreviation for following, the one that sends a reader on to the next page
rust is the corrosion iron gets
to rate something is to estimate its value

annotation.surface: A news line: work stopped once somebody's estimate of the corrosion came in.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Following' looks like a link word saying which piece goes after which, and is a letter of the answer instead. That single letter is the whole difference between two ordinary words and the long one they build.
annotation.definitionFit: To frustrate a plan is to stop it getting any further forward, which is halting its progress.

entries.clue: Key rings for climbing can be stiff (6)

indicatorNotes.rings: to ring something is to draw a circle round it, so the letters named first close on the ones named next
indicatorNotes.climbing: in a down entry what climbs is read up the column, so the letters come out in the opposite order

blocks.note: Esc is the escape key, top left on every keyboard
to be pro something is to be for it

annotation.surface: Key rings sold to climbers, and a complaint that they can be stiff.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Key' is the one on a keyboard rather than a door key or a musical scale, and 'for' is the little word PRO. Two of the shortest words in the clue carry all six letters, and the whole assembly is then read upwards.
annotation.definitionFit: A stiff is slang for a dead body, named for the rigidity that sets in a few hours after death.

entries.clue: Falls asleep creating clue for dons? (4,3)

blocks.note: the straight half: the head drops and sleep arrives without anybody going to bed
the other half describes what the answer would do if you met it in a crossword: read as wordplay, its first word's letters treated as its second word demands give DONS

annotation.surface: Somebody dozing off in the middle of writing a clue about university dons.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second half as a description of the answer rather than a meaning of it. Setters call this a reverse anagram, and a clue that talks about clues is the usual signal that one is coming.
annotation.definitionFit: To nod off is to drop into sleep where you sit, the armchair kind rather than going to bed.

entries.clue: Tip up open vase (8)

blocks.note: an overt act is an open one, done where anybody can see it
an urn is a vase, usually the big-bellied sort

annotation.surface: Somebody tipping over a vase that stands open.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tip up' in a down entry looks exactly like an instruction to turn something round, and here it is the definition, with nothing reversed anywhere. Two everyday words, joined end to end, is the whole of the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: To overturn a thing is to tip it up until it lands the other way about, which is what happens to a vase or a verdict.

entries.clue: Excelled partly through dishonesty (5)

indicatorNotes.partly through: a stretch taken part of the way through a word is some of its letters and not all, read in the order they already stand

blocks.note: the five letters wanted run from the third letter of the word to the seventh

annotation.surface: Somebody who did brilliantly, and did it partly by cheating.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface accuses its achiever of cheating and the wordplay quietly agrees, keeping the praise inside the dishonesty. 'Excelled' is past tense and so is the answer, which is the check that settles which word here is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: To shine at something is to do it outstandingly well, so shone is excelled put in the past tense.

entries.clue: Hand parts in Fidelio's opening to awful singer (7)

indicatorNotes.opening: the opening of a word is where it starts, so only its first letter is wanted
indicatorNotes.awful: an awful mess is a mess all the same, and letters in a mess are not in the order they were handed over

blocks.note: Fidelio is Beethoven's only opera, and just its first letter is taken
the six letters of SINGER put back in another order

annotation.surface: A dreadful singer taking the stage at the start of Fidelio.
annotation.walkthrough: The italics round Fidelio mark it as a title, which is the hint that the word is there to be used rather than understood. An anagram that leaves five of its six letters adjacent is the hardest sort to see.
annotation.definitionFit: Fingers are the parts a hand divides into, four of them plus the thumb.

entries.clue: Opposition politicians in Norway tucked into the cod prepared with wasabi (6,7)

indicatorNotes.tucked into: to tuck a thing in is to push it down out of sight, so the letter named lands buried among the others
indicatorNotes.prepared: food prepared is food chopped and rearranged, and letters get the same treatment

blocks.note: six letters of fodder, article included
six more letters of fodder
N is Norway's international vehicle letter, the one on the oval sticker

annotation.surface: Norway's opposition MPs tucking into a cod dish served with wasabi.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tucked into' reads as eating and works as burying, which is how a single letter disappears into twelve others. The shadow cabinet is the opposition's front bench at Westminster, each member paired against the minister whose job they would take.
annotation.definitionFit: The shadow cabinet is the team of opposition spokespeople in Parliament, politicians who shadow the government ministers one for one.

entries.clue: Very regularly catches fever, getting increasingly woozy (6)

indicatorNotes.regularly: letters taken at a regular interval means every other one, counted from the start
indicatorNotes.catches: to catch a thing is to take hold of it and keep it, so what follows is kept inside

blocks.note: the first and third letters of VERY, taken every other step
an ague is a fever, the shivering malarial kind

annotation.surface: Somebody who keeps catching fevers and is growing groggier with each one.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Very regularly' is one phrase in the surface and two separate things underneath: a word to take letters from, and the rule for taking them. Ague is an old name for a fever that now survives mainly in crosswords.
annotation.definitionFit: Woozy carries the muddled, out-of-focus sense as well as the dizzy one, so something growing woozier is growing vaguer.

entries.clue: Blue cycling shoe boxes needed for dance parties (8)

indicatorNotes.cycling: a cycled word sends its letters round the loop, the one at the front going to the back
indicatorNotes.boxes: to box a thing is to shut it in a box, so the letters named first close round the ones named next

blocks.note: SHOE with its front letter sent round to the back
somebody blue is feeling down

annotation.surface: A blue cycling shoe, boxed up, is what the party needs.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Blue cycling shoe' is a single object in the surface and three separate instructions under it, one of them the colour. A hoedown is an American country dance, the square-dancing sort with a caller and a fiddle.
annotation.definitionFit: A hoedown is a rowdy country dance and the party built round it, so the plural names several such knees-ups.

entries.clue: Discovered parcel of asparagus seed (3)

indicatorNotes.Discovered: read as dis-covered, the word has had its covering taken off, so the outside letters go

blocks.note: a parcel here is a portion, and the portion asparagus comes in is a spear, meaning one stalk

annotation.surface: A parcel of asparagus seed turns up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Discovered' is doing its cryptic work as dis-covered, stripped of a covering, while the surface reads it as found. Asparagus is counted in spears the way celery is counted in sticks.
annotation.definitionFit: A pea is the seed of the pea plant, the thing you sow as well as the thing you eat.

entries.clue: Hirsute officer set about devouring contents of egg (6)

annotation.definitionNote: 'Contents' is plural where the answer is singular: the setter means the one occupant a fertilised egg is carrying, not a list of ingredients.

indicatorNotes.set about: to set a thing about is to turn it round, so the letters are read the other way along
indicatorNotes.devouring: what is devoured goes down whole and out of sight, so the words in front hold the letters inside them

blocks.note: the run straddles the two words, hir|SUTE OF|ficer, and is then read backwards

annotation.surface: A hairy officer starting in on the contents of an egg.
annotation.walkthrough: A hidden run written backwards is the hardest kind to spot, because the eye scans left to right and finds nothing. 'Set about' means began in the surface and turn it round in the wordplay, and the same three-letter word does both.
annotation.definitionFit: A foetus is the developing creature a fertilised egg carries, so what such an egg contains is exactly this.

entries.clue: Stupid fellow was first held back smuggling wild animal (8)

indicatorNotes.held back: what is held back does not go forward, so those letters run the other way
indicatorNotes.smuggling: a smuggler carries the goods hidden inside something else, so the letters named next travel within

blocks.note: whoever was first led the field
an otter is a wild animal, and the five letters go in whole

annotation.surface: A fool who once led the field is stopped with a wild animal on him.
annotation.walkthrough: The dotterel is a small plover, famously tame and easy to catch, and its name was transferred to anybody equally easy to take in. The animal buried in the answer is a different creature from the bird the answer names.
annotation.definitionFit: A dotterel is a byword for a dupe or simpleton, the bird's reputation for being caught without a struggle having attached itself to people.

entries.clue: Indonesian resident's limitless bank loan (4)

indicatorNotes.limitless: a thing without limits has no edges, so each word named after it gives up its first and last letter

blocks.note: BANK with the letters at either end taken off
LOAN treated the same way

annotation.surface: A bank loan with no ceiling, offered to somebody living in Indonesia.
annotation.walkthrough: One instruction covers both words that follow it, which is easy to miss while the second is busy looking innocent. The anoa is a dwarf buffalo found on Sulawesi and nowhere else on earth.
annotation.definitionFit: The anoa lives only in Indonesia, on Sulawesi, so calling it a resident of the country is literally true of the animal.

entries.clue: Extremely abstruse answers developed knowledge (9)

indicatorNotes.Extremely: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so the first and last letters are all that is taken
indicatorNotes.developed: something developed has grown into a shape it did not have, and letters do the same

blocks.note: the first and last letters of ABSTRUSE
seven letters of fodder

annotation.surface: Very obscure answers that grew into something like knowledge.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' reads as an intensifier bolted onto the word after it, and is the instruction to take that word's two ends. Seven letters plus those two ends makes nine, the count worth doing before trusting any long anagram.
annotation.definitionFit: Awareness is what you have once you know a thing is there, so it stands for knowledge in the loose general sense.

entries.clue: Lost again, rekindling homesickness (9)

indicatorNotes.rekindling: to rekindle is to get a fire going again out of what is already lying there, and these letters are relit in another arrangement

blocks.note: nine letters of fodder, exactly the length wanted

annotation.surface: Somebody lost once more, and an old feeling flaring up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Again' is the decoy: it looks like the instruction to rearrange, and it is fodder, while the real signal is the word about relighting. Nostalgia was coined by a doctor for homesick Swiss soldiers, and the fond looking-back came later.
annotation.definitionFit: Nostalgia was built from the Greek for homecoming and pain, and homesickness is the ache it originally named.

entries.clue: Stamping out (8)

blocks.note: what a mint does to a blank disc of metal to turn it into a coin
said of a workforce that has downed tools and left the building

annotation.surface: Stamping out something unwanted.
annotation.walkthrough: Coins are struck from blanks, which is the stamping, and a workforce that is out is on strike. A clue of two words almost always means two definitions, because there is no room for anything else.
annotation.definitionFit: Striking is stamping in the minting sense, a coin struck from a blank, and a workforce that is out has downed tools and is striking.

entries.clue: Unpopular revenue generator possibly shares around excessive returns (5,4)

indicatorNotes.around: to go around a thing is to close outside it, so the letters named first sit either side of the ones named next
indicatorNotes.returns: what returns comes back along the way it went, so the letters are read from the far end

blocks.note: a part in something is a share of it
deep carries the sense of far past the usual degree, as in deep trouble or a deep discount

annotation.surface: An unpopular money-spinner handing its shareholders excessive returns.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Returns' is the money word the surface needs and the turn-it-round instruction the wordplay needs, and it comes last, so the whole assembly flips at the end. British drivers habitually accuse the authorities of siting these to raise money rather than save lives.
annotation.definitionFit: A speed trap fines the drivers it catches, so it raises money and is loathed by those paying; 'possibly' marks it as one example of the type.

entries.clue: Fictional character likely to be first in identity parade? (7)

blocks.note: everybody standing in a line-up is a person, whatever else they may be
A heads the alphabet, so the one given that label stands at the front of the row

annotation.surface: Wondering which invented character would be picked out first in a police line-up.
annotation.walkthrough: An identity parade is the British name for a police line-up, and the people in one are labelled A, B, C along the row. The second half of the clue describes the answer's own two halves rather than defining it.
annotation.definitionFit: A persona is the character an author or a performer puts on, an invented person standing in front of the real one.

entries.clue: One working hard starts to subedit world-renowned books (4)

indicatorNotes.starts to: the start of a word is its first letter, and the plural takes one from each of the words named

blocks.note: the first letter of each of the two words
OT is the Old Testament, the books a setter means when the word stands alone

annotation.surface: A subeditor beginning work on some world-renowned books.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Books' is one of the fixed crossword signals for part of the Bible, OT for the Old Testament and NT for the New. A swot is British school slang for somebody who studies harder than their classmates think decent.
annotation.definitionFit: A swot is one who works relentlessly at their books, and the word is school slang rather than a compliment.

entries.clue: Disregard poetry in Old English (7)

indicatorNotes.in: what is in something sits inside it, so the letters named before go within the ones named after

blocks.note: verse is poetry
O for old and E for English, two of the commonest single-letter stand-ins

annotation.surface: Some poetry written in Old English.
annotation.walkthrough: Old English is one language in the surface and two separate abbreviations underneath, split down the middle. Chambers lists 'to overlook, to fail to notice' beside the everyday sense, and that older meaning is the one the definition uses.
annotation.definitionFit: Beside the familiar 'supervise', oversee keeps the older sense of overlooking a thing, letting it pass unnoticed, which is what disregarding it is.

entries.clue: Have an ambition of rents rising in emergency accommodation (6)

indicatorNotes.rising: in a down entry what rises is read up the column, so those letters come out backwards
indicatorNotes.accommodation: to accommodate is to find room for somebody, so the letters named alongside make room inside for the rest

blocks.note: A&E is the accident and emergency department of a British hospital
a rent in cloth is a rip, and the four letters then go in upwards

annotation.surface: Rents going up on emergency housing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Emergency accommodation' is a phrase about housing the homeless in the surface and two separate jobs underneath, a hospital department and an instruction to make room. Rents here are tears in cloth, not monthly payments.
annotation.definitionFit: To aspire is to hold an ambition and reach towards it, so having one is what the word describes.

entries.clue: Two taking time finishing off regional chart for auditor's drawings (8)

indicatorNotes.taking: to take a thing in is to receive it inside, so the letters named before open to let the next one sit among them
indicatorNotes.finishing off: what finishes a thing off comes at its very end, so this piece is added last
indicatorNotes.for auditor: an auditor is somebody who listens, so the word before is to be heard rather than read

blocks.note: a chart is a graph, and 'regional' points at the short-A accents in which it is said graff
two written in Roman numerals
t is time on any physics formula sheet

annotation.walkthrough: The front half is heard rather than spelt, which is why the PH comes out as FF. 'Two' is the Roman pair I and I, a device worth filing away, because a stray I on its own almost never looks like part of an answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Graffiti are the drawings and scrawls sprayed on walls, so the plain word covers them, and the setter takes the plural as it comes.

entries.clue: Wrongfully insert leader of uprising to begin with (5)

indicatorNotes.leader: a leader goes at the head of things, so this piece takes the front of the answer
indicatorNotes.uprising: in a down entry what rises goes up the column, so those letters are read backwards

blocks.note: the clue's own little word, taken as it stands and then turned
to begin with is first, and first written as a numeral is 1st, the figure standing in for the I

annotation.surface: Wrongfully slipping the ringleader of a revolt in, to start with.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Leader of uprising' reads as one phrase about a revolt and is three separate jobs underneath, none of them a person. A number written as 1st, 2nd or 3rd is a standing invitation for a setter to read the figure as a letter.
annotation.definitionFit: To foist something on somebody is to slip it in where it has no business being, which is inserting it wrongfully.

entries.clue: Closed up cell, finally having eased suspect outside (6)

indicatorNotes.finally: the final letter of the word before it is the only one taken
indicatorNotes.suspect: something suspect is not what it claims to be, and these letters are not in the order they claim either
indicatorNotes.outside: what is outside goes round the outside, so these letters close on the one named before

blocks.note: five letters of fodder
the last letter of CELL

annotation.surface: A cell finally emptied, the suspect eased outside.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Suspect' is the adjective meaning dodgy, not the noun the police-station surface wants, and it is the word doing the shuffling. The comma after 'cell' has to be ignored, because it falls in the middle of a single instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Something sealed has been closed up so that nothing gets in or out, as an envelope or a jar is.

entries.clue: Move quickly to pinch a small quantity of spirits (3)

blocks.note: to dart off somewhere and be back in a moment
a sharp squeeze between finger and thumb
a third definition in the same row: the small measure of whisky poured against the cold

annotation.surface: Dashing out to steal a quick drop of whisky.
annotation.walkthrough: Three definitions in a row rather than the usual two, with 'to' the only word doing nothing but join them. Two are verbs and the last is a noun, which is legitimate as long as each on its own means the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Covering all three: to nip somewhere is to go there briskly, to nip is to give a sharp pinch, and a nip is a small measure of spirits.

entries.clue: The same rodents overwhelming Illinois home (8)

indicatorNotes.overwhelming: to overwhelm is to come over a thing and cover it entirely, so the letters named before close over the ones named next

blocks.note: do. is the written abbreviation for ditto, meaning the same again
mice are rodents, and the four letters open to take the state
IL is the two-letter postal abbreviation for Illinois

annotation.surface: Mice swarming over a house somewhere in Illinois.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The same' is DO, from the ditto mark written do. in old ledgers, and it is the piece that leaves the first two letters unexplained until you have met it. Illinois gives IL, the code Americans put on an envelope.
annotation.definitionFit: A domicile is the place somebody lives, the legal word for the home a person is counted as belonging to.

entries.clue: Take in tongue-in-cheek broadcast (6)

indicatorNotes.broadcast: what is broadcast goes out as sound, so the words before it are to be heard rather than read

blocks.note: to say a thing tongue-in-cheek is to say it in jest, and those two words run together into one

annotation.surface: A joking remark that went out on air.
annotation.walkthrough: The homophone works on a whole phrase rather than a word, which is why the clue and the answer look nothing alike on the page. 'Broadcast' can signal sound or scattered letters, and the clue offers no letters to scatter.
annotation.definitionFit: To ingest something is to take it into the body, so taking it in is the plain phrase for the same act.

entries.clue: Excellent American directions (3,2,2)

annotation.definitionNote: 'American' is not part of the meaning but a label on it: the exclamation is a US one, and the setter marks it so that a British solver knows which register to search.

blocks.note: the shout of approval an American gives when somebody has done well
the route to take, with the three words read flatly

annotation.surface: An American giving excellent directions.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Way to go!' is the American shout of approval, which is why the setter attaches the nationality; read flatly, the same three words are the route somebody should take. Three-word clues leave no room for wordplay, so two definitions is the likeliest shape.
annotation.definitionFit: Said as an exclamation it means well done, excellent; read literally it is the way to go, which is what a set of directions tells you.

entries.clue: Lie around in bed, getting behind schedule (7)

indicatorNotes.around: letters thrown around land anywhere, so the word named before comes out in another order
indicatorNotes.in: what is in something sits inside it, so these letters go within the word named next

blocks.note: the three letters that open to take the rest
a lie is a tale, and those four letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: Somebody lounging in bed and running later by the minute.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lie around' is one idea in the surface, lounging, and two instructions underneath, one naming letters and one shaking them. 'In bed' looks like where the lying happens and is where the letters go.
annotation.definitionFit: Something belated arrives after the time it was due, which is what being behind schedule means.
